people are more likely to accept positive than negative feedback, that they are more likely to reject positive feedback that they perceive to be inaccurate, and that the likelihood of accepting or rejecting positive feedback increases as a function of the degree to which the feedback corresponds to a self-representation.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

people's reactions to evaluations of themselves are determined by the interplay of three factors: (1) the valence of the evaluation, (2) the perceived veracity of the evaluation, and (3) the perceived cost and benefit of accepting the evaluation.
the search for beauty and truth, which is an inherent part of the human condition, is the driving force behind the cognitive operations people perform to evaluate themselves.
the positive tropism is an important first phase of processing that is followed by a verisimilitudinal analysis, and if resources and motivation are sufficient, by a cost-benefit evaluation.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
people have a positive tropism for positive evaluations of themselves, and that this tendency is moderated by the extent to which they are motivated to engage in a veridical search for truth.

the search for beauty and truth is a framework for understanding the reactions to evaluations of the self, and it is based on the notion that people are motivated to seek positive evaluations of themselves, but also to seek accurate evaluations of themselves.
we have found support for a three-stage process in which people's reactions to evaluations are influenced by the positivity and verisimitude of the evaluation.
The main takeaway from our work is that
positivity and verisimitude, two fundamental desires of human cognition, are the key drivers of how people process evaluations.
people's desire for positivity is a fundamental cognitive bias that is not necessarily in conflict with their desire for truth.

the search for beauty and truth is a complex and multi-faceted process, and that it is best understood in terms of a sequence of cognitive operations that are triggered by the mere identification of an evaluation.
